<Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, Rep. Adriano Espaillat>: We appreciate the efforts of Chairman Valadao and his staff in producing the Fiscal Year 2027 Legislative Branch bill. While the bill incorporates several Democratic priorities, it ultimately fails to adequately fund the needs of the Legislative Branch and includes a partisan policy rider that undermines Congress's constitutional responsibilities and institutional independence.
The interim allocation for the Legislative Branch totals $7.3 billion, slightly more than one-half of one percent above the Fiscal Year 2026 enacted level. Consistent with longstanding practice, under which each chamber determines its own housekeeping requirements and the other concurs without intervention, the House bill does not include funding for the Senate or Senate office buildings. Excluding Senate items, the bill provides $5.4 billion, which is $125 million, or 2.2 percent, below the Fiscal Year 2026 enacted level and $1.2 billion below the budget request.
These funding levels are insufficient to meet the operational and infrastructure needs of the Legislative Branch. With such a constrained allocation, the bill fails to adequately fund critical projects managed by the Architect of the Capitol that are necessary to address the deterioration of House office buildings and broader campus infrastructure. Delaying these investments will only increase long-term costs and further jeopardize the safety, functionality, and preservation of the Capitol complex.
The funding levels, combined with the inclusion of the partisan policy rider in section 116, are unworkable, and Democrats cannot support the legislation as drafted. Most notably, the bill proposes nearly a 25 percent cut to the Government Accountability Office (GAO).
Weakening GAO weakens Congress's ability to hold the Executive Branch accountable and ensure taxpayer dollars are spent as intended. The proposed reduction would force GAO to eliminate more than 1,000 positions, severely undermining the workforce responsible for audits, investigations, and oversight conducted on behalf of Congress.
The Committee considered an amendment that would have struck section 116, a provision restricting GAO's ability to bring independent civil actions under the Impoundment Control Act of 1974 unless Congress first adopts a concurrent resolution authorizing such action. The amendment failed.
The inclusion of this provision undermines Congress's constitutional oversight authority by limiting GAO's longstanding independent enforcement role under the Impoundment Control Act, authority that has existed for more than fifty years and was reaffirmed by Congress following the Supreme Court's decision in Bowsher v. Synar. These concerns are particularly significant given GAO's ongoing investigations into whether the Administration unlawfully withheld fiscal year 2025 appropriated funds. At a time when strong oversight is essential, the bill both weakens GAO's enforcement authority and proposes nearly a 25 percent cut to the agency responsible for identifying waste, fraud, abuse, and unlawful executive actions across the federal government.
The bill also reflects the Majority's refusal to adopt amendments to prohibit certain judgment fund payments to elected officials and to permit Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients to receive compensation as employees of the Legislative Branch.
The Legislative Branch bill should not be used to weaken Congress's oversight capacity or undermine the independence of the institutions that support its constitutional responsibilities. Instead, this legislation should provide the resources necessary for Congress to function effectively as a coequal branch of government, conduct meaningful oversight, safeguard the Capitol complex, and serve the American people. Because this bill fails to meet those standards, Democrats cannot support the legislation as drafted.
Rosa DeLauro.
Adriano Espaillat.
